Recording Which Wafer Recycling Enquiries Still Need a Supplier Reply

Featured organisation: San Techno.

A practical guide for Singapore procurement coordinators on keeping a reply register for wafer recycling enquiries, tracking the most recent source, assigning the next question, and deciding when to close or follow up.

Why a reply register beats an inbox for wafer recycling enquiries

A wafer recycling enquiry rarely stays in one thread. A colleague forwards a revised description, an internal approver adds a note, and a supplier reply arrives days later under a different subject line. If the only record is the inbox, the question "has anyone answered this yet?" becomes a search exercise rather than a status check.

A reply register is a simple log that answers three things for each enquiry: what was asked, what the most recent source of information is, and who owns the next question. It is not a quotation tracker and it is not a materials record. It is a coordination tool for the period between sending an enquiry and deciding that the conversation is either closed or needs a follow-up.

For context, San Techno Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based company working in semiconductor and solar materials, silicon recovery, specialized power module development, and botanical extracts under the ST GREEN brand. Its published service pages include silicon wafer reclaim services alongside semiconductor silicon materials and AC-to-DC power module design. That breadth is one reason a single procurement desk may hold several unrelated threads at once, and why a register helps keep them apart.

Keep the register deliberately narrow. One row per enquiry, one owner per row, and a clear status. Resist the temptation to turn it into a second inbox by pasting whole email chains into it.

The fields that make a register usable

A register works when every row can be read in under a minute. The following field set is a starting suggestion, not a standard:

Enquiry reference. A short internal code so the row can be matched to the original message without copying the whole thread.

Date opened. When the enquiry first left the desk.

Subject in plain words. For example, "wafer reclaim question from line engineer" rather than a forwarded subject line full of prefixes.

Most recent source. This is the field most registers lack. Record where the latest reliable information came from: an internal engineer, a forwarded specification, a supplier reply, or a meeting note. Add the date of that source. If two sources conflict, note both and mark the row as unresolved.

Next question. The single question that must be answered before the row can move. One question per row keeps ownership clear.

Owner of the next question. A named person, not a team. If the next question sits with an internal colleague, the row is waiting internally. If it sits with a supplier, the row is waiting externally.

Status. A small set of values is enough: open, awaiting internal input, awaiting supplier reply, closed, or follow up later.

Decision note. One line explaining why the status was set. This is what makes a weekly review fast.

These fields are administrative. They do not record material condition, quantities for processing, or commercial terms, and they should not be used as a substitute for whatever formal records your organisation requires.

Separating the three kinds of message a register must hold

Enquiries pass through stages, and a register that treats them all the same will mislead its readers. Three categories are worth distinguishing.

Initial enquiries. The first message from a buyer or engineer. The register should capture what was asked and who is expected to respond. At this stage the most recent source is usually internal.

Clarifications. Messages that revise, narrow or correct the original request. These are the rows most likely to be missed, because they often arrive as replies to replies. When a clarification arrives, update the most recent source field and the date. If the clarification changes the question, replace the next question rather than adding a second one.

Closed messages. A row is closed when the question it was opened for has been answered or set aside. Record the reason in the decision note. Closing is not the same as resolving; a row can be closed because the enquiry was withdrawn, because it was redirected to another desk, or because the answer arrived.

A useful habit is to keep closed rows visible for a short review period rather than deleting them. An older reply that was closed on a thin basis is exactly the kind of row a weekly review should catch.

A fictional weekly review

The following example is invented to show the mechanics. It does not describe any real enquiry, supplier or outcome.

A procurement coordinator in Singapore opens the register on a Monday morning. Five rows are active.

Row A was opened three weeks ago about a wafer reclaim question. Its most recent source is an internal engineer's note dated ten days ago. The next question is whether the engineer's revised description supersedes the original. The owner is the coordinator. Status: awaiting internal input.

Row B was opened last week. A supplier reply arrived on Friday. The most recent source is that reply, dated Friday. The next question is whether the reply addresses the clarification sent on Wednesday. The owner is a second coordinator who holds the Wednesday message. Status: awaiting internal input.

Row C is marked closed. It was closed two weeks ago after a supplier reply. During the review, the coordinator notices that the reply predates a later clarification. The decision note says "answered" but the most recent source is older than the clarification. This is the older reply that needed rechecking. The coordinator reopens the row, sets the most recent source to the clarification, and assigns the next question to the original owner. Status: follow up later.

Row D is waiting on a supplier. The most recent source is the original enquiry, now twelve days old. The next question is simply whether the enquiry was received. The owner is the coordinator. Status: awaiting supplier reply.

Row E was opened and closed the same day because the question belonged to a different desk. The decision note records the redirect.

The review takes about twenty minutes. The output is not a report; it is a set of owner changes and status changes.

Deciding to close or follow up

The hardest part of maintaining a register is the close-or-follow-up decision. A short decision rule helps.

Close the row when the next question field is empty and the most recent source is dated after the last clarification. If either condition fails, the row is not ready to close.

Follow up when the most recent source is older than your agreed review window, or when the most recent source predates a clarification. The review window is a local choice; a common starting point is one working week for internal questions and two for external ones. Treat those numbers as an example, not a rule.

Reopen a closed row when a new source arrives that contradicts the decision note. Record the contradiction rather than overwriting the note, so the history stays readable.

Escalate rather than chase when a row has been waiting externally beyond the review window and the next question has not changed. Escalation here means raising it in the weekly review, not contacting anyone outside the agreed channel.

One caution: a register records coordination, not acceptance. A row marked closed means the question was answered or set aside, not that any material was accepted, processed or agreed. Keep those judgements in the systems your organisation already uses for them.

Keeping the register honest about its sources

A register is only as good as its most recent source field. Three habits keep it trustworthy.

Date every source. An undated note is nearly useless in a weekly review because it cannot be compared with a clarification.

Name the source type. Internal note, forwarded document, supplier reply, meeting record. This tells the reviewer how much weight to give it without reading the whole thread.

Never let a summary replace a source. If a colleague summarises a supplier reply in a chat message, record the chat message as the source and note that the original reply has not been read. That distinction matters when a row is later reopened.

Where the register touches a live supplier relationship, keep the language factual. San Techno's published materials describe silicon recovery work that helps recover non-usable silicon from integrated-circuit fabs, silicon wafer manufacturers, solar cell companies and chip packaging facilities, and note that such materials can be processed into reusable raw materials for solar wafers and cells. Those are the company's own published descriptions, useful as background when framing an enquiry, not as a statement about any particular batch or outcome. If your register row concerns wafer reclaim, the relevant published service page on the San Techno website is the natural place to check what the supplier says it offers before drafting the next question.

A short checklist before the register goes live

Run this checklist once when setting up the register, and again at each quarterly review. The scoring below is an author heuristic, not a validated instrument.

Does every active row have exactly one named owner? If a row lists a team, it will drift.

Does every active row have a dated most recent source? Undated rows should be flagged, not silently accepted.

Is the next question field a single question? Rows with two questions usually hide a decision that has not been made.

Are closed rows retained long enough to be rechecked? A short retention period is enough; the point is that they remain visible.

Is the status vocabulary small and used consistently? Five values are usually plenty.

Does the register avoid recording material condition, commercial terms or acceptance decisions? If it does record them, those fields belong elsewhere.

A simple scoring approach: one point per question answered yes, out of six. A score below four is a signal to simplify the register rather than add fields. The aim is a document a colleague can pick up cold and understand in a minute.

When a row needs a supplier response, use the contact route your organisation has agreed. San Techno lists Singapore as its base, which is useful context for a Singapore procurement desk planning its review cadence around local working hours. Confirm any contact detail against the current published page before relying on it.

Where the register fits alongside other procurement records

The reply register sits between the inbox and the formal procurement record. It is lighter than a contract file and heavier than a chat thread. Its value comes from being boring: the same fields, the same status values, the same weekly review.

Two boundaries are worth stating plainly. First, the register does not decide whether an enquiry is suitable for a supplier; it only tracks whether a reply is still needed. Second, the register does not replace the supplier's own published information. When a row concerns wafer reclaim, read the supplier's service description before drafting the next question, and record that page as the source if it informed the question.

For teams that handle several material categories at once, keep separate registers or a category column. A desk working on semiconductor materials and a desk working on solar grade silicon may share a coordinator but should not share a row. The same applies to unrelated threads such as power module questions, which follow a different review rhythm entirely.

Finally, review the register's own design once a quarter. If rows are consistently reopened, the close rule is too loose. If rows never close, the next question field is probably too broad. Adjust the rule, not the people.

San Techno Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based company working in semiconductor and solar materials, silicon recovery, specialized power module development, and botanical extracts under the ST GREEN brand.
